How to keep cool in a heatwave: 25 tips from the people who know best, from a Rio lifeguard to an Egyptian archaeologist
For some, scorching days and humid nights are just the norm. So how do they stay chilled and comfortable?
Get up and out
Luis Pacherrez Antón is president of Agroperu Cooperative, a democratic collective of 102 small-scale farmers in the Chira River valley, Peru. He is based in Piura, known as “the city of eternal heat” because it stays hot and dry all year round. “The sun rays start to shine very early – from 9am,” he says. “So as people who work in cultivation, under a burning sun, we stay comfortable by starting much earlier and consuming the healthy foods that we produce, like bananas, oranges, lemons, grapes, papayas and avocados.”
Obada Almaitah, a diving instructor and course director in Aqaba, Jordan, says that summer temperatures regularly reach 40C, and can exceed that during heatwaves. “The sun is very strong, humidity is generally low and UV levels are high for much of the year, so I schedule physically demanding tasks during the early morning whenever possible.” When temperatures soar, flip your schedule to do chores before work – and forgo that weekend lie-in; instead, mow the lawn or lug shopping home first thing.
Tour guide Despina Savvidou has been leading visitors around the Acropolis of Athens for 48 years. She has witnessed first-hand the difference climate breakdown has made. “It’s like I’m in another country,” she says. “Thirty or 40 years ago, 32C was very hot; now 32C is normal. Two years ago, we had a heatwave that lasted two weeks.” Savvidou advises people to book on to her earliest tour – before the Acropolis even opens. “We have a tour that begins at 7.45am. We give a short introduction, and as soon as the doors open we go in. Between 8am and 10am – even if it’s 40C – it’s OK.”
Don’t wait until you’re thirsty to drink
This is a common tip from people who work in the baking sun, like Egyptian archaeologist Dr Zahi Hawass, who has worked at sites in the Nile delta, the Western desert and the Upper Nile valley. “The weather in Egypt during the summer is extremely hot, especially at archaeological sites such as Saqqara,” he says. “I make sure to drink water regularly while working outdoors. In the heat, it’s important not to wait until you feel very thirsty, but to keep drinking throughout the day.”
Sherene M El-Sioufi, a doctor in pulmonary and sleep medicine, lives and works in Jeddah, which experiences some of the hottest and most humid conditions in the world. She says: “In Saudi Arabia, many people drink laban, a yoghurt-based drink that provides hydration and electrolytes. The key is to drink consistently.”
Sip, don’t guzzle
“We tell people to drink little by little: at 10am take two sips, at 10.15am two more,” says Savvidou. “I have at least 15 glasses of water a day, but slowly.” Luiz Eduardo Dos Santos Nascimento, a lifeguard in Rio de Janeiro, where temperatures can exceed 40C during heatwaves, says: “I always keep a water bottle nearby and stay constantly hydrated during my shift.” John Napolo, a wildlife protection services manager at Etosha Heights Wildlife Monitoring Unit in Namibia, where summer temperatures can exceed 40C, says: “Each ranger carries five litres of water for the day. We drink three or four and pour the remainder on our heads when the heat is too much.”
Tip water on your head
Speaking of which, Prof Ollie Jay,director of the Heat and Health Research Centre at the University of Sydney, recommends this approach to cool down quickly: “When you apply water to the skin it evaporates, which cools you down, because it does the same job as sweating, but without the physiological stress of having to sweat. If you drink half your water and tip the other half over yourself, you get much more effective cooling.”
Dr Youssouf Moussa of the International Organization for Migration in Obock, Djibouti oversees humanitarian operations in a region facing extreme heat – in the week we speak a heat alert warns that temperatures could reach 53C. He uses “practical methods such as lightly wetting clothes, which helps cooling through evaporation”. To quickly cool an adult or child so they are comfortable enough to sleep, El-Sioufi suggests “a cool damp cloth on the neck, wrists or forehead”.
… Or ice your neck
Wondered why tennis players sit with ice towels around their necks? Jay and his team came up with an extreme heat policy for Tennis Australia. “Our studies showed that ice towels cool a relatively large area of the body in a small window, as a player spends just 80 seconds sitting in their chair.” Simply wrap crushed ice cubes in a rolled up wet towel and place it around your neck.
Take warm showers
For a speedy refresh, Savvidou swears by “a warm shower – no Greek person has a cold shower and most of us get under the water two or three times a day. I shower at 10am, again at 4pm, just to refresh without soap, and again before bed.” El-Sioufi also advises taking a shower before bed – a lukewarm one. “Many people assume a cold shower is best, but a lukewarm shower allows the body to cool gradually.” Michael Haindongo, a guide at Etosha Heights, who patrols this Namibian wildlife reserve daily, walking up to 500km (311 miles) a month and living in a camp in the bush for three-month rotations, takes a bedtime lukewarm shower, and when the temperature soars: “I wet a large towel and lie on it, and keep windows and doors open if there’s no threat from animals.”
He describes how houses in his village are naturally ventilated as they are thatched with grass and walls are made from wood, which is “semi open”. He also says “the Ovahimba people apply red ochre on their faces and any body parts exposed to the sun”. This natural cosmetic, made from butterfat and red ochre, provides protection against UV rays, thanks to high iron oxide content.
… Or play in a bucket
The village of Lytton in British Columbia became the hottest place ever in Canada for three days running in June 2021, reaching 49.6C. Dr Michael Schwandt is a medical health officer in the region. He says that to quickly cool small children, “one of the best things is immersion. It doesn’t need to be total, just getting their legs into a bathtub – or even a bucket. Similarly, placing cool, damp cloths on the body can help it to evaporate heat. That could be a flannel, a muslin or a lightly damp T-shirt – it shouldn’t have to be freezing cold, just cool.”
Down tools at peak times
“For humanitarian teams, rest is essential to stay safe and effective when working outside for extended periods in extreme heat,” says Moussa. “From noon until 3pm we limit movements to what is strictly necessary, although in case of an emergency, we remain fully available.” Haindongo isn’t “too sure if there’s such a thing as feeling comfortable working in the heat – we tolerate it, and would rather work early mornings and afternoons, or if necessary by moonlight.”
Federica Salvo, who runs the Giardino della Kolymbethra garden in Sicily, notes a similar approach: “Sicily holds the record for the highest temperature ever recorded in continental Europe – 48.8C on 11 August 2021.” She describes how Sicilians felt “overwhelmed” during that heatwave. “It was hard to work, or to concentrate on anything.” Fortunately, there are rules in place to protect people. “Throughout summer, work is prohibited from 12.30pm to 4pm in the construction and agriculture sectors, and during working hours workers are encouraged to take long breaks in the shade.”
Eat light, a little later
“If you have a big dinner, you suffer – you sweat and you don’t sleep,” says Savvidou. “On a hot day, for dinner I’ll have apricots, cherries and banana in yoghurt with raisins. For lunch, we cook vegetables – green beans, okra, peppers, aubergine – in olive oil with feta cheese and serve it with a big salad. In Greece, there is no meal without a salad. For lunch today, I grilled fish and served it with a salad of cucumber and tomatoes, and that’s it – no potatoes, no rice, no pasta.”
Carmen Vallejo Carmona, a grandmother in Seville – known as the frying pan of Spain thanks to sweltering summer temperatures – says her hot weather diet is “based around salads and cold dishes. The gazpacho in our town is more liquid, drunk from a glass. We also eat salmorejo (another chilled Andalucían soup), boquerones en vinagre (marinated anchovies), vegetables and the occasional ice-cream. Lunch is late – normally between 2pm and 3pm – and dinner is after 9pm, once the worst of the heat is gone.”
Moussa says: “In extreme heat we avoid heavy meals, especially at midday. Instead, we focus on light, water-rich foods and drink plenty of fluids, including tea. A typical breakfast includes lahooh, a soft flatbread, with tea and water. On the coast near Obock, Red Sea fish grilled Yemeni-style is very common.”
Eat to hydrate, too
Dr Rashmi Sarkar is a dermatologist in New Delhi, where summer daytime temperatures commonly reach 42-45C. She says: “Traditional Indian diets include many foods considered to be cooling and hydrating: yoghurt, chaas [buttermilk], coconut water, fresh fruits such as watermelon and mangoes, and cucumbers. Drinks such as lemon water, jaljeera [a spiced beverage], aam panna made from raw mango, [cordials such as] khus and sattu are popular because they help replace fluids and electrolytes.”
Almaitah says: “During long diving days, I replace electrolytes naturally through foods such as melon, cucumbers, tomatoes and yoghurt.” Nascimento notes that “it’s common in Rio for people to consume coconut water, natural juices and chilled fruit”; while Napolo says: “Some rangers have traditional knowledge of plant roots and tubers that can give you extra water.” If you want a root veg with a high water content for salads, radish is 95% water, while celeriac, carrot and beetroot are all 88%.
Remember, less isn’t always more
“One of the biggest misconceptions is that less clothing is better,” says El-Sioufi. “Many traditional practices – including wearing loose, flowing garments – evolved for a reason. They provide excellent protection from direct sunlight while allowing air circulation.” Napolo agrees: “The best way to stay cool is to be completely covered – long sleeves and trousers, and something to cover your face. The key is to have light, loose layers that allow airflow as you move.” Savvidou opts for cotton trousers that “are so wide you don’t know where the leg is, a loose shirt, and no belts. People think they need everything open in the heat, but this isn’t wise because you get dehydrated.”
Duong and Van, Vietnamese grandparents who live in Nam Dinh, where it’s very hot and humid, also cover up. “At home we wear shorts, loose dresses, vests, and men are topless, but when travelling by motorbike, people wear a full outfit on top of their normal clothes that covers their whole body, face and hands. It’s made of cotton.” Moussa also opts for light, loose, breathable clothing that protects the skin while allowing air to circulate. “In Djibouti, traditional clothing is well adapted to the heat. Women often wear pygama, a long, loose, lightweight dress, while men wear the futa, a cotton wrap that allows airflow.”
Don’t forget accessories
Sarkar wears sunglasses with UV protection, and when outdoors for longer periods a broad-brimmed hat, scarf or dupatta(long, shawl-like cloth), and she carries an umbrella. Savvidou would love to carry a parasol, “but it’s windy on the Acropolis, and we lose them. Hats make you sweat, so we wear visors, because they protect your face from the sun, but your head is in the air.”
Duong and Van say battery-powered fans have taken off in Vietnamese cities but “people still use paper fans, and some use the traditional Vietnamese hat as a fan”. For Vallejo Carmona, her traditional hand fan “comes everywhere with me. It’s a very Sevillano thing.” She also opts for “light footwear, preferably made of leather, so the foot can be naked and fresh”.
Stop fantasising about air con
If you were guiltily Googling the cost of installing an air-conditioning unit mid-heatwave, Jayhas news for you: “There are many more sustainable ways to cool down. We have AC at home, but we haven’t turned it on in years. We installed ceiling fans, which work a treat. The more airflow you get across the skin the better, so if you’re lying on a bed, a ceiling fan is probably best; if you’re at a desk, a pedestal fan.” Salvo concurs: “When it’s very hot, I sleep with the fan on. I try to avoid the air con.”
Shutter up
You’ve heard all about closing the curtains, but here’s how it’s viewed where it has been a custom for generations. Salvo says: “In Italy, tradition has taught us to close the shutters during the day to keep the house dim and shield it from the sun, keeping it cooler. We then open the windows early in the morning and in the evening when the air cools down.”
Romel Bernal, an architect in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, where recent temperatures have reached 38C, has a nifty tip: “Blackout curtains help a room retain its temperature when not in use during the day, while light-coloured linen materials offer a cooling effect – and if you mist them with water, the evaporation keeps them cool.”
Get a thermometer
Schwandt recommendsinvesting ina thermometer “to get an objective measure of when it’s OK to open windows”. Jay agrees, saying, “We’ve installed a temperature sensor inside and another outside so we can look at the difference. That way, we can keep the windows open when it’s cooler outside than in, and when that flips, we shut the windows.”
Sit under a tree
As the climate heats up, nature can provide excellent relief. “The temperature on our forecast is measured in the shade, so if you’re out in the sun you’re exposed to 12 to 15 degrees higher heat load when you take into account the extra radiation,” says Jay. “Sitting under a tree is a nice way of getting shade. Grass also dampens the absorption of radiation, which is another moderating effect. Depending on the type of tree, you have the evapotranspiration effect, where water in the leaves evaporates and reduces ambient temperature by a couple more degrees celsius.” It’s why, says Haindongo, when the heat gets too much, “I lie under a tree, or climb to the hilltop for the breeze.”
… Or create shade with canopies and drapes
“You can achieve a microclimate in any home by taking advantage of natural resources, like plants and trees that create shade and absorb the impact of the heat. Landscape design has gone from being a luxury to being essential,” Bernal says. Vallejo Carmona describes how internal patios in many houses in Seville are “covered by thick fabric to create shade and coolness, and the council covers some streets with awnings to avoid the direct sun and create shade”.
Jay notes that while you can create shade in your garden, you must couple it with decent ventilation. “Some people create shade that blocks the prevailing wind, and then you get hot, because there’s no airflow.” Think sails or awnings, but choose heavy fabrics, as “some fabrics let radiation through because they’re not a tight enough weave,” he says.
Use mulch
Salvo says increasing temperatures are changing the way people garden. “Gardeners and farmers are increasingly using mulch to reduce evaporation. By practising this ancient method, we can increase soil water retention, protect roots from extreme heat and provide plants with more nutrients. We are also choosing more drought-resistant species, such as olive trees, lavender, rosemary, sage and Mediterranean native plants.”
Start ’em young
Australia has been incredibly successful at bringing skin cancer rates down among younger people, while here in the UK they are continuing to increase. It’s why starting some basic rules early is a great idea. “When Australian kids go to school, they have wide-brimmed hats and are not allowed to go out in the playground if they don’t have them on,” says Jay. “These very strong rules around sun safety start as early as five, and by the time you’re an adult, putting sunscreen on is like putting your underpants on – everybody does it every day.”
Stay safe in the water
Horribly, heatwaves are often coupled with drownings, so safety in the water is paramount. “Many people enter the sea unprepared after long periods in the sun, some after consuming alcohol, and end up ignoring the risks of currents, depth and sea conditions,” says Nascimento. “It’s important to respect lifeguard signals, swim in protected areas and never enter the sea alone. Extreme heat also increases physical strain on the body, so it’s necessary to recognise its limits.”
Almaitah says that “many people underestimate sun exposure because they feel cool in the water, but the combination of direct sunlight and reflection from the sea can cause severe sunburn, especially on boats, where exposure can be continuous”.
Socialise later
“We socialise as much as possible,” says Vallejo Carmona, “but during the hours of the worst heat, between 1pm and 6pm, most families are at home. After dinner, once it’s cool, neighbours gather with chairs to chat on the pavements outside, so by the time we go home to sleep, our houses are fresh.”
Duong and Van “sit out in the evenings to have trà đá, a traditional tea, but instead of having it hot in a cup, we dilute it in a big glass and put lots of ice in. It’s a lovely, traditional way of people having some cool air outdoors and socialising after a day of hiding from the heat.”
Slow your pace
“When I was doing my PhD, I did a field study in Seville in summer,” says Jay. “I immediately noticed that people moved more slowly and walked close to the side of a building to get shade.” Nascimento concurs: “Control your pace – it’s important to manage your energy throughout the day.” Almaitah says: “People often try to continue normal activities, but in very hot weather it’s important to slow down, stay hydrated, seek shade regularly and listen to the body’s warning signs.”
Moussa has similar advice – “We adapt by working early in the morning or later in the day, and prioritising essential tasks” – but says there’s another side to it: “We work in extreme conditions, yet every day we also see hundreds of migrants crossing this same desert with access to nothing: no water, no shoes, no shelter. Some of our energy comes precisely from that, from the drive to help someone who has less than you do.”
Lower your expectations of sleep
“The body naturally needs to cool slightly before sleep begins, so when temperatures remain above 40C, that becomes more difficult,” says El-Sioufi. “People often take longer to fall asleep, wake more frequently and spend less time in restorative deep sleep. Infants and young children are especially vulnerable, because their ability to regulate body temperature is less developed. Parents should be flexible and, rather than focusing on exact nap durations, ensure children remain hydrated, cool and comfortable.” Schwandt also says parents need “openness to changing schedules – because kids will go pretty close to flat out before they stop. Move playtimes to early morning and late evening, and recognise that oftentimes kids won’t fall asleep easily because of the heat, and that can transmit to fatigue the next day.”
Adapt your home
Rather than a total overhaul, Bernal recommends that you “reduce the impact of the heat in the areas of the home most used by its inhabitants”. Cross ventilation is crucial, so open windows and doors at opposite ends of your home and leave spaces clear to allow air to flow. “You can integrate technologies like windows with double and triple glazing, and windows with protective overhangs to minimise solar exposure. Outdoors, choose white for facades directly exposed to the sun and sand and beige tones for flooring, as they don’t cause glare or reflect heat.” Cement tiles, terracotta, light-coloured cantera stone and brushed-finish marble are excellent choices for preventing outside surfaces from overheating, and are suitable for walking barefoot.
And finally … splash about
Pacherrez Antón shares that “in Piura, during the summer, we have carnavales, where neighbours, tourists and the whole population gather, and water tanks and hoses are used to spray everyone as they dance and enjoy themselves”. Even if you are miles from Peru’s city of eternal heat, a local splash park or fountain should do the trick … just not at midday!

Southern Sask. heat wave expected to last all week as air quality drops
Heat and smoke warnings were issued for parts of Saskatchewan on Saturday. (Image Credit: Environment Canada website)
Moodie said in the south of the province is where most warnings are and said they will last until next weekend.
“You may see a break for a day or two, but in general, we’re going to see highs in the 30s till next weekend,” she said.
The warning criteria is not just related to the daytime heat, but also that things won’t really cool down much at night.
“The criteria we have for our heat warnings is daytime highs of 32 and lows of 16. We also have a humidex criteria of 38. Those overnight lows are not allowing people to cool their houses if they don’t have air conditioning,” Moodie said.
Some regions under heat warnings are also getting smoke.
“Yesterday we had some smoke from the fires in B.C. spread into southwestern Saskatchewan, and we are expecting that to linger over the next few days.”
Potentially the smoke could spread through southern Saskatchewan into southeastern Saskatchewan, Moodie said. Environment Canada says that air quality and reduced visibility due to wildfire smoke can fluctuate over short distances and can vary considerably from hour to hour.
“Wildfire smoke can be harmful to everyone’s health even at low concentrations,” the alerts say.
“People with lung disease (such as asthma) or heart disease, older adults, children, pregnant people and people who work outdoors are at higher risk of experiencing health effects caused by wildfire smoke.”
EC said people may experience mild and common symptoms such as eye, nose and throat irritation, headaches or a mild cough and anyone experiencing shortness of breath, wheezing, severe cough, dizziness or chest pains should stop outdoor activities and contact a health care provider.
They advise that when indoors, people should keep windows and doors closed as much as possible and to protect indoor air from wildfire smoke by using a clean, good quality air filter in your ventilation system or a portable air cleaner that can filter fine particles.
Both agencies said people should limit time outdoors as much as possible, and wearing a well-constructed, well-fitting and properly worn respirator type mask (such as a NIOSH-certified N95 or equivalent respirator) can reduce exposure to fine particles in the smoke. Even though exposure may be reduced, there can still be risks to health.
People more likely to be impacted by outdoor air pollution include those aged 65 and older, pregnant people, infants and young children, people with an existing illness or chronic health condition, and people who work outdoors, should reduce or reschedule strenuous activities outdoors and seek medical attention if experiencing symptoms.
More information on air quality alerts for specific areas of the province is available at weather.gc.ca.
Information is also available on the Saskatchewan Public Service Agency website at saskpublicsafety.ca and the SaskAlert app. The provincial air quality summary for Saskatchewan can be found here.
Hot temperatures, which can feel hotter because of high humidity, bring with them a risk of heatstroke and heat exhaustion.
The Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA) says classic heatstroke can develop without exertion when a person is exposed to a hot environment and the body is unable to cool itself effectively. The body’s ability to sweat and transfer the heat to the environment is reduced. and a person with heatstroke may stop sweating.
Classic heatstroke may develop over several days, and babies, older adults, and people with chronic health problems are at the greatest risk.
Exertional heatstroke may develop when a person is working or exercising in a hot environment. A person with heatstroke from exertion may sweat profusely, but the body still produces more heat than it can lose. This causes the body’s temperature to rise.
“These people have altered levels of consciousness. They’re dizzy, they’re confused, they’re maybe going in and out of consciousness and they’ve stopped sweating,” family physician Dr. Carla Holinaty told 980 CJME in 2023.
“They just don’t have that capacity anymore and now their skin is dry.”
Heatstroke is a medical emergency and people should call 9-1-1 as soon as they notice someone showing signs of heatstroke.
After calling for help, Holinaty said it’s important to cool the afflicted person down by moving them to a cool, shady place or using cold, wet towels to lower their body temperature.
“I wouldn’t be trying to get them to drink a whole lot of liquid, especially if they’re quite confused or kind of coming in and out of consciousness, because we don’t want them to choke,” she said.
Heat exhaustion is milder than heat stroke.
“We tend to see people get headaches or muscle cramps. Sometimes they get nauseous. Sometimes they might feel a little bit dizzy or weak,” Holinaty said. “Their body temperature is not so high that it’s dangerous.”
The SHA says heat exhaustion occurs when you can’t sweat enough to cool your body. It can develop when you work or exercise in hot weather and don’t drink enough liquids to replace the fluids you lose from sweating a lot. Heat exhaustion can be caused by loss of fluid (dehydration) or loss of electrolytes.
Symptoms of heat exhaustion include fatigue, weakness, headache, dizziness, and nausea. Also, the skin is pale, cool, and moist.
Mild heat exhaustion may sometimes cause fainting but it doesn’t cause a change in your mental alertness and usually can be treated at home.
SHA says that heat-related illnesses include:
Take action to protect yourself and others – extreme heat can affect everyone’s health. Determine if you or others around you are at greater risk of heat illness. Check on older adults, those living alone and other at-risk people in-person or on the phone multiple times a day.
Watch for the early signs of heat exhaustion in yourself and others. Signs may include headache, nausea, dizziness, thirst, dark urine and intense fatigue. Stop your activity and drink water.
Heat stroke is a medical emergency. Call 9-1-1 or your emergency health provider if you, or someone around you, is showing signs of heat stroke which can include red and hot skin, dizziness, nausea, confusion and change in consciousness. While you wait for medical attention, try to cool the person by moving them to a cool place, removing extra clothing, applying cold water or ice packs around the body.
—

Mumbai rain to continue till Monday as IMD issues yellow alert; showers likely to ease from Tuesday
Mumbai is expected to receive heavy rain until Monday, with the IMD issuing a yellow alert for Mumbai and Thane and an orange alert for Raigad. Rainfall intensity is likely to reduce from Tuesday, while the city's reservoirs have reached 86% of their total storage capacity.
Mumbai is likely to continue witnessing rain until Monday, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issuing a yellow alert for Mumbai and Thane districts and an orange alert for neighbouring Raigad district. However, the weather department has indicated that rainfall intensity is expected to reduce from Tuesday, with only moderate showers likely across most parts of the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, as per Indian Express.
The city woke up to overcast skies on Sunday as intermittent rain continued through the day. According to IMD data, Colaba recorded 20 mm of rainfall between Saturday and Sunday morning, while the Santacruz observatory received 7.2 mm. Thane recorded 23 mm during the same period.
In Navi Mumbai, Belapur recorded 37 mm of rainfall, followed by Koparkhairne (36 mm), Nerul (31.4 mm), Vashi (24 mm), Airoli (20 mm) and Digha (15.4 mm).
Rainfall activity eased by Sunday evening, with Santacruz recording only 1 mm of rain while the Colaba observatory reported no rainfall during that period.
According to report, the IMD has forecast heavy rainfall at isolated places in Mumbai and Thane on Monday. Raigad district, including Navi Mumbai, is expected to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall, prompting the weather department to issue an orange alert.
Meteorologists attributed the ongoing spell to a shear zone associated with a low-pressure system along India's west coast, which has increased moisture inflow and intensified rainfall across the Konkan region and parts of Gujarat.
However, IMD scientists said monsoon activity is likely to weaken gradually after Tuesday. While Mumbai, Thane and Palghar are expected to receive only moderate rainfall from Tuesday onwards, Raigad is likely to remain under a yellow alert until the end of July.
The ongoing monsoon revival has significantly boosted seasonal rainfall in the city. Between June and July 26, the Santacruz observatory recorded 1,884 mm of rain, accounting for nearly 80% of Mumbai's annual average rainfall of 2,319 mm.
Heavy rainfall has also improved the city's water reserves, with the combined storage in Mumbai's seven lakes reaching 12.47 lakh million litres, or 86% of their total capacity, as per Indian Express.

articles.full_text:
Disclosure: This website may contains affiliate links.
St. Vincent’s Government recently revealed its 90 day Emergency Relief Package designed to protect the general public from increasing costs of living.
However, despite the Government’s publicized efforts to aid the public, Vincentians have been burdened with what they believe will be record breaking electric bills as they question how much of this relief is actually making it to the people; or whether Utility Companies are being protected at the expense of Consumers.
On May 27th, 2026 Prime Minister Godwin Friday introduced the program. As part of the program, the Customs Service Charges and Excise Taxes on Diesel Fuel used in generating Electricity would be removed. This measure will result in the loss of $1.65 Million in Foregone Revenue for a 3-Month Period.
The Administration maintained that these savings should be passed along to Households and Small Businesses. Unfortunately, the practical effects of this announcement have resulted in a dramatic spike in Electric Costs.
During June 2026 the “Fuel Surcharge” reached an all-time High of .7378 Dollars per Kilowatt-Hour (kWh) exceeding the previously recorded mark of .6927 kwh established in July 2022.
Notably, this new All-Time Record was achieved during the same time period that the Tax Waivers were in place and there existed a Subsidy.
It became clear in July 2026 that the problem had intensified dramatically when St. Vincent Electricity Services Limited increased the Fuel Surcharge to .8320 Dollars/kWh (an increase of approximately 9 Cents from June).
Vinlec maintains that the Fuel Surcharge is merely a “Pass-Through” Cost and therefore does not generate Profit. However, the continued escalation of Rates suggests that the Financial Cushion for Consumers is ultimately failing to provide meaningful Relief.
The Governments Relief Strategy uses a Tiered System. In essence, Vinlec only provides Matching Contributions if the Fuel Surcharge Exceeds specific Thresholds of .710 per kWh and/or .770 per kWh.
For those Vincentians who are experiencing difficulties stemming from Global Inflation these Triggers may not be sufficient to avoid the difficult decision of Paying for Power or Purchasing Basic Grocery Items.
Further, the National Cost of Living Task Force has been instructed by the Government to Monitor Prices Weekly.
Specifically, the Task Forces’ Oversight will ensure that Tax Reduction Benefits do not simply inflate Business Profit Margins but are instead passed on to Consumers.
The necessity for such Monitoring Highlights Concern that the $1.65 Million in Tax Relief may be Absorbed into Large Entity Operational Structures while Everyday Citizens continue to see their Bills Increase.

articles.title: Extreme heat increases the risk of workplace injuries across Canada - The Conversation

articles.full_text:
For millions of Canadians, those warnings changed day-to-day plans. For many workers, though, the workday continued on construction sites, farms and loading docks, and inside factories, warehouses and restaurant kitchens.
The most visible workplace consequences are heat exhaustion and heat stroke. But heat also creates a less obvious and poorly understood risk: it makes ordinary workplace injuries more likely.
Official counts likely understate the problem, since heat is often the contributing factor rather than the injury named on the claim form.
Canadian evidence shows how easily this burden can hide in plain sight. A peer-reviewed study linked 374,078 accepted workers’ compensation claims in Québec with daily temperatures from 2003 to 2010.
The study found that, for every 1 C increase in the daily maximum temperature, the workplace injury rate rose by about 0.2 per cent. That sounds small, but it accumulates across a heat wave and a large workforce. The increase occurred in both indoor and outdoor industries.
A recent nationwide U.S. study reached a similar conclusion. Researchers geocoded more than 845,000 injury reports and matched them with daily weather conditions.
Compared with a heat index of 80 F (about 27 C), the odds of injury were three per cent higher at 90 F (32 C), 10 per cent higher at 100 F (38 C) and 20 per cent higher at 110 F (43 C). The researchers estimated heat caused roughly 28,000 additional workplace injuries across the U.S. in 2023.
These findings challenge the idea that heat is mainly an outdoor-work problem. Outdoor workers face direct sun and humidity, while indoor workers contend with ovens, machinery, poor ventilation and inadequate cooling. Heavy exertion and protective clothing further increase the body’s heat load.
Protections vary across provinces
Canada has no common minimum standard for protecting workers from extreme heat. Every province and territory requires employers to protect health and safety, but the rules vary considerably.
B.C., for example, requires employers to assess heat exposure and create a control plan when workers may be at risk. The rules call for engineering controls where feasible and for cool drinking water.
Québec sets exposure limits using the wet-bulb globe temperature, which combines temperature, humidity, radiant heat and air movement, and prescribes controls once those limits are reached.
Ontario and Alberta rely more heavily on broad employer duties, hazard assessment and official guidance rather than on province-wide standards.
Federally regulated workplaces are also changing: new thermal-stress rules have been adopted but will not take effect until February 2027 — too late to protect workers this summer.
Other provinces and territories have no heat-specific legislation at all, leaving the issue to fall under employers’ general duty to protect worker health and safety. A general duty states the desired outcome, but it doesn’t say when a hot day requires action or what that response should include. Protection then depends on employers’ knowledge, resources and willingness to act.
Rules need triggers and enforcement
Evidence on regulation is encouraging, but it also warns against symbolic rules. A recent peer-reviewed study compared heat-related deaths among California’s outdoor workers with those in neighbouring states.
California’s initial 2005 heat standard was not linked to fewer deaths. After enforcement intensified in 2010, researchers estimated a 33 per cent reduction in heat-related deaths. After the rules were strengthened again in 2015, the estimate rose to 51 per cent, reflecting the stronger rules and continuing enforcement. Neither period’s estimate was statistically significant on its own, but the two post-2010 periods combined were.
The lesson is not simply to “have a heat rule.” Effective protection requires clear triggers, practical controls and enforcement.
Separate research tracking California workplace injuries from 2001 to 2018 found that estimated injury burden caused by heat fell by about 30 per cent after 2005. The researchers could not identify the cause, but said the finding suggests workplaces may be able to reduce heat-related risks using existing practices and safety practices.
Federal, provincial and territorial governments in Canada should establish a common minimum standard covering indoor and outdoor work. Employers should be required to assess heat using temperature, humidity, radiant heat, workload and protective clothing, and to prepare written response plans. Plans should include water and cooled rest areas, paid breaks, gradual acclimatization, training, and emergency and stop-work procedures.
Workers should help design these plans, since they often know where heat accumulates and which production pressures make breaks difficult to take.
Employers should not wait for legislation. Heat is a foreseeable workplace hazard and the controls needed to manage it are well understood. Telling workers to drink more water is no substitute for redesigning schedules, workloads and workplaces.
Canada’s heat waves are becoming a recurring test of how the country protects its workers. If extreme heat is predictable, the injuries it causes should not be treated as unforeseeable or unpreventable.
